subject: Banking
title: Deposit Insurance: Savior and Enabler
description: Learn Deposit Insurance: Savior and Enabler in one minute.

hook.text: FDIC insurance ended bank runs but created moral hazard. Depositors stopped checking if their bank was safe.

buildup.text: Before FDIC, depositors closely watched their bank's health. Insurance removed the incentive to monitor bank behavior.

discovery.text: Banks take bigger risks because insured depositors don't flee. Only uninsured depositors create market discipline.

twist.text: SVB proved the limits. 96% uninsured deposits created massive run risk that insurance wasn't designed to cover.

climax.text: Deposit insurance is essential but imperfect. It prevents panic at the cost of reducing accountability.

punchline.text: Stops bank runs. But removes the incentive for depositors to watch their bank.

quiz.question: What is the downside of deposit insurance?
options: It reduces depositors' incentive to monitor bank health

details.summary: Deposit insurance was created in 1933 to end bank panics by guaranteeing customer deposits. While it has largely succeeded in preventing runs, critics argue it also enables reckless bank behavior by removing depositor discipline.
details.whyItMatters: Deposit insurance is the foundation of modern banking confidence. Without it, bank runs would be common. But the guarantee also means depositors have no incentive to monitor whether their bank takes foolish risks.
takeaways: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank
Bank runs virtually disappeared after deposit insurance was introduced
The 2023 SVB crisis showed the system's limits when uninsured deposits dominate

faq.question: How does deposit insurance prevent bank runs?
faq.answer: When depositors know their money is guaranteed by the government, they have no reason to rush to withdraw during a scare. This eliminates the self-fulfilling panic where rational fear of a run causes the actual run.

faq.question: Does deposit insurance make banks take more risks?
faq.answer: Yes, this is a well-documented moral hazard. When depositors' money is guaranteed, they do not bother checking if their bank is taking excessive risks. Banks can attract deposits with high rates funded by risky investments, knowing the FDIC backs the deposits.
